newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar vulnerable despite late buying.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar vulnerable despite late buying.

text.p: The Australian dollar staged a late recovery from a move towards support, but remained within sight of its 1997 lows as eroded rate differentials and a strengthening mark weighed on the unit, traders said.

Since falling over one cent on Friday in response to an unexpected cut in official interest rates, the dollar steadied around US$0.7650, holding a easier bias in local trade on Monday as selling for marks added to the pressure from the rate cut.
By 5.00 p.m (0700 GMT) the dollar had risen off its lows of US$0.7638 to be at US$0.7762/67. This was almost level with its early US$0.7663/68, but down on a Friday close of US$0.7680/85.

"It's a good sign it's not falling out of bed, but it's not a good sign that it's not bouncing. I'd say its still in limbo at these levels," one trader said, saying there had been talk of mark buying against the dollar adding to the negative sentment.

The local dollar's pattern of gradually easing before late buying was also reflected on the crosses, where it ended at 88.80/90 yen and 1.2913/25 marks, from openings of 89.00/10 and 1.2893/05 and Friday closes of 88.89/99 yen and 1.2987/3000 marks.
The mark strengthened as a result of a strong showing by leftist parties in the first round of French elections.
With the voting leading to some speculation over European union, the mark benefitted across the board, posting strong rises in Tokyo against the yen and U.S. dollar.
Traders said the mark buying kept the pressure on the dollar, which which was stabilising after a dramatic one cent fall in the wake of Friday's rate cut.
The easing took local rates to 5.50 percent, to be level with the U.S. Fed Funds rate for the first time in 14 years.
With rates in other countries, such as Japan and Britain, also seen having an upward bias, the Australian dollar no longer retains the attractiveness of high yielding status to investors.
On the downside, initial support was expected in the US$0.7600/20 zone, with a break here clearing the way for a move to US$0.7550, the low seen so far this year.
That low came in February, and represented the trough of a two month downtrend from the previous rate cut in December, as markets speculated on the likelihood of another rate cut.
Bullish words from RBA Governor Ian Macfarlane in February had eased fears, and markets remained of the view that rates were on hold until caught out on Friday.
Against the negative factors, a firmer tone to commodity prices should act as a floor for the dollar.
As well, analysts said the outlook for low inflation, cited by the RBA as a factor allowing them to reduce interest rates, could keep real rates high.

"The fact that the markets maybe aren't factoring in lower inflation in Australia, to the extent that they begin to do that it basically revises up our real rates here in Australia, which can support the currency as well," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist David Bassanese said.
Following the rate cut, data this week has lost some of its edge, especially that which will help finalise first quarter GDP forecasts.

However, Tuesday's private new capital expenditure figures for the first quarter will still be important as they will give an indication of whether expectations of four percent growth in 1997 will be achieveable.
